'''''Calystegia silvatica''''' ('''large bindweed''') is the largest species of [[Calystegia|bindweed]] and is a strong rampant climber. It is native to southern Europe but has been introduced to many other areas because it is an attractive garden plant. ''Calystegia silvatica'' subsp. ''fraterniflora'' <small>(Mack. & Bush) Brummitt</small> ('''short-stalked false bindweed''') is native to North America.<ref>[https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?406420 Germplasm Resources Information Network. Beltsville (MD): United States Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service. Retrieved 2016-09-22.]</ref>

It has large, arrow-shaped leaves and showy white trumpet-shaped flowers up to 9 centimeters in diameter. It is considered a [[weed]] in some areas where it has [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] and now grows wild. It spreads easily via hardy [[rhizome]]s. There are several subspecies.

==Description==
Large bindweed is a [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] that twines in a counter-clockwise direction to a height of up to 5 m. The [[leaves]] are arranged alternately on the spiralling stem on petioles up to 15 cm. The leaves are dull green above and paler below, simple and sagittate (arrowhead shaped), up to 15 cm long and up to 9 cm wide.<ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The [[flower]]s are white, sometimes narrowly pink on the outside only, produced from late spring to the end of summer (between July and September in northern Europe). The buds are enclosed by large (4.8 cm long), ovate, green [[bracts|bracteoles]] pouched at the base; during [[anthesis]] they strongly overlap.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref> The open flowers are trumpet-shaped and 6–9 cm diameter. After flowering, the [[fruit]] develops as an almost spherical capsule, which is hidden by the bracts. It is 1 cm in diameter, containing two to four large, dark brown or black [[seed]]s that are shaped like quartered oranges.<ref name="Sell3" />
[[File:Calystegia silvatica 2020-02-08 8011.jpg|thumb|right|A ripe fruit]]
[[File:Calystegia silvatica kz4.jpg|thumb|right|Pink-flowered variety]]

==Identification==
The best way to separate large bindweed from hedge bindweed (''C. sepium'') in flower is by the bracteoles, which subtend the flower and wholly or partially encompass the sepals. Large bindweed has short, wider bracteoles which overlap where they meet, whereas hedge bindweed has narrower, longer ones which leave a gap between them, allowing a glimpse of the sepals.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |title=Plant Crib |date=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}}</ref>
{{Image frame|width=424|content=[[File:Calystegia sepium bracteoles.jpg|200px]] [[File:Calystegia silvatica bracteoles.jpg|218px]]|caption=Bracteoles of hedge bindweed (left) and large bindweed (right)|align=center}}

Vegetatively, large bindweed can be distinguished from [[Calystegia sepium|hedge bindweed]] by the shape of the sinus - the gap between the lobes at the base of the leaves. The former has a U-shaped sinus, in contrast to the usually V-shaped one in the latter.<ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>
{{Image frame|width=400|content=[[File:Calystegia sepium vs silvatica sinus.jpg|400 px]]|caption=Leaves of hedge (left) and large bindweed (right)|align=center}}

==Taxonomy==
Common names include "morning glory" (a name which is shared with hundreds of other species) and "giant bindweed".<ref>{{BSBI 2007|access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref>
